content:
We're pleased to announce the first official release of Lean 4.

  • Release notes are at https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/releases/tag/v4.0.0
  • You can now use the toolchain leanprover/lean4:4.0.0. Mathlib master has just bumped to it!
  • There is a post on the Lean community blog about future release cycles.

Try it out ourself:

% lake +leanprover/lean4:stable new my_stable_project
% cd my_stable_project
% cat lean-toolchain
leanprover/lean4:4.0.0
% lean --version
info: downloading component 'lean'
Total: 174.3 MiB Speed:  11.2 MiB/s
info: installing component 'lean'
Lean (version 4.0.0, commit ec941735c80d, Release)

Exciting news!

We're not at the point that we can promise backwards compatibility between versions, beyond documenting all breaking changes in our RELEASES.md.

With regards to this, is lean committed to semver? Can we expect that breaking changes will lead to major version bump (i.e., lean 5.0)?

Regular releases

The plan at this stage is to create a new "minor" version (i.e. v4.1.0, v4.2.0) approximately each month. There will be a release candidate v4.1.0-rc1 early in each month, and if all goes well that will become the stable version at the end of the month. Further release candidates will be made if we find something broken, and sometimes also just to make new features available to Mathlib faster.

We're hoping that Mathlib is able to begin tracking release candidate toolchains, rather than nightly toolchains.

At this point the "patch" version (the 0 in v4.2.0) will be unused: it's space to grow later.

We're not at the point that we can promise backwards compatibility between versions, beyond documenting all breaking changes in our RELEASES.md. As Lean and the Lean ecosystem matures we will update this approach.

from the blogpost
Btw I notice that the time on the blogpost is in six hours! A timezone issue?

Also, from experience in the LLVM community: even mature communities can life on main and do not necessarily need point releases. I think it is worth considering if we really want release-candidate development. In particular, the cost of maintaining point releases and especially fixing bugs in them might be better invested in fixing main. Also, a delay of a months for fixes in main to end up in mathlib, could be painful. I guess this is not the place to deeply debate this, but I wanted to place this seed of thought to make sure the decision to do point-releases is taken with awareness of other options.

Most important, I am glad lean 4.0 has been released!

@Eric Rodriguez That does not answer my question? Or you're saying that this implies that indeed, breaking changes will come in lean v5.0?
They're still planning to make breaking changes, and it all seems it will be released in the minor version. I also feel there's a certain level of branding in the 4.
Plenty will be broken in 4.1.0. :-) But we will try to make sure we explain the breakages in RELEASES.md!
In this announcement at LFCTM2023 (Password: LftCM2023), Sebastian Ullrich made it fairly clear that the 4 was unlikely to go anywhere!
To summarize my understanding of the Lean versioning scheme: we have Lean x.y.z where x is the constant 4 and z is the constant 0.
Perhaps that will change in the future, but yes, that is the scheme. We intend to have 4.X.0-rcY as well, but most people shouldn't need to notice these.

From the download page, https://leanprover.github.io/download/:

Lean 4
Lean 4 is currently released as milestone releases towards a first official release.

The main point about Lean 4 was made in the Q&A after the announcement. Unfortunately, I didn't capture the Q&A in the recording. Sorry about that.
The point was: Lean 4 took six years of development, which is longer than it took for all previous versions combined.
(Of course that's only tangentially related to the question of version numbering conventions.)

Eric Wieser said:

In this announcement at LFCTM2023 (Password: LftCM2023), Sebastian Ullrich made it fairly clear that the 4 was unlikely to go anywhere!

From 1.3.4 A Short History of Lean in An Extensible Theorem Proving Frontend ( @Sebastian Ullrich 's thesis ) :

Given the frequency of major Lean releases with almost no backward compatibility, inevitably the question arises: when will we switch to Lean 5 and start from scratch again? While the need for a subsequent major version is impossible to project so early into the life cycle of a new release, we can at least take the escalating time between releases as a hint towards stability, especially considering that the implementation of Lean 4 took roughly as long as that of all three versions before it combined. I think I can speak for all core developers that at this point, we do not even want to think about any effort that comes close to the Lean 4 rewrite. In many ways, the foundations of Lean 4, particularly the extensible frontend, are as generic as we can make them and there are no plans to revolutionize them yet again.

Terminology is a bit overloaded here. Semver (which I don't like at all, get off my lawn) takes "new major version" to mean "breaking changes were made", while in Sebastian's dissertation "major version" means "start over from scratch". But in the future Lean may adopt a versioning scheme where Lean 5 could exist without a full rewrite, and I think this is the spirit of the original question.
Also, as Sebastian notes in that quote, the frontend is generic enough that it is hopefully that it will not ever need a true "from scratch" rewrite, but rather just incremental improvements.

Just noting: v4.1.0 of Lean is out.

In fact, so is v4.2.0-rc1, and Mathlib is already using it. In particular you will find many improvements in Lake, including substantially faster performance!
(We're a bit early this month for various reasons: we intend that v4.2.0 will land end of October.)
